# Disseminated zoster:
Patient presented with zoster rash over the L5 dermatome of his
LLE. The lesions had partially crusted over at presentation.

protection and transferred to the MICU. The unresponsiveness may

dementia. After patient was intubated, his mental status

support from the ventilator. Patient was extubated the next day
without weaning and did well.
.

discontinued 24 hrs later). Lumbar puncture was performed,
showing a lymphocytic meningitis indicative of a possible zoster
meningitis. CSF fluid was apparently not plentiful enough to be
suitable for VZV or HSV PCR, so these tests could not be
performed. Patient was placed on Acyclovir 10 mg/kg (700 mg IV
TID), for a course to be continued for 21 days total. Concern
was also given to possibility of pneumonitis, hepatitis,
ophthalmicus, and Ramsay Hunt. ID consult felt that patient's
CXR was not indicative of VZV pneumonitis. CT chest was not
performed, as treatment would not change if pneumonitis were
present. LFTs were wnl. Patient developed a rash over his eyes,

zoster ophthalmicus. Patient had a right lower facial droop that
resolved after several days of admission. Patient's LLE rash
continued to resolve throughout admission. Patient was not
placed on steroids for concern of immunosuppression, and patient
has no post-herpetic neuralgia complications. Patient was
hydrated with NS 3L per day, since acyclovir can cause renal
failure.

the L picc was removed.

labs wnl.

   Critical Care
   89 yo with a history of recurrent aspiration, Parkinson's, dementia and
   weight loss brought to ED by EMS after being witnessed to aspirate by
   home health aid.  In ED in respiratory distress, hypotensive leading to
   intubation, CVL placement and volume resuscitation.  Rx'd with broad
   abx after blood, urine sputum cx.  In ICU his exam is notable for
   stable VS with BP near baseline (~90s) on a low dose of levophed, but
   HR 90 and making urine. Chest exam remarkable for active exhalation
   with marked insp and exp efforts and obvious auto-PEEP on the
   ventilator.  We are continuing abx but will narrow spectrum awaiting gr
   stain and sputum cx.  We are increasing sedation and PEEP in an attempt
   to make him more synchronous with the ventilator.  His chest X-Ray and
   exam suggest diffuse bronchial/parenchymal inflammation consistent with
   chemical bronchitis/pneumonitis more than a bacterial pneumonia.  His
   troponin is flat and he is volume responsive making cardiac
   decompensation unlikely.  Nevertheless we will continue ruling out for
   MI and will check echo this adm.
   Total time spent:  65 minutes
   Patient is critically ill.

because he had fever, AMS, and rhabdo, however it was unclear
why he would have had hypotension if that was the explanation.

because he was prescribed adderall and multiple seratonergic

dysfunction and worsened pulm HTN, but he had RV dysfunction in

stable enough for CTA or V/Q scan and was unlikely to be able to
tolerate anticoagulation given he was also in DIC with active
bleeding.
.

continued to rapidly deteriorate despite aggressive
resuscitation efforts. His blood pressure was not able to be
maintained despite fluids and multiple pressors. Lactic acid was
high on presentation and continued to rise up to 16. He had
respiratory failure requiring intubation. His laboratory
findings were suggestive of DIC and he required cryo, FFP, and
blood transfusion. During the hospitalization he developed
bleeding from the rectum, bladder, and mucous membranes. He had
severe acute kidney injury and associated electrolyte
derangements. He also had evidence of shock liver.
Rhabdomyolysis was presents as well which could be explained by
toxidrome but unusual for septic shock.
.

to decline. After discussion with the patient's son [**Name (NI) 382**] and

want prolonged intubation or resuscitation if he had a small
chance of returning to his previous level of functioning. A
decision was made to make the patient CMO and take the patient
off of the ventilator. He passed away shortly thereafter.
.
# Respiratory failure/Hypoxia: Most likely this was ARDS from
shock. CT chest showed some small peripheral wedge-shaped
infiltrates, which could have been infarcts. He was not stable
enough for VQ scan or CTA.
.
#Altered Mental Status: infection (CNS vs. pulmonary) vs.

amphetamines/opioids, however he was on adderall and opioids at
home. NCHCT did not show any acute process.  Neurology was
consulted and recommended MRI although patient was never

of the left carpus and hand. When she was first seen, she had
a very small forearm. She elected distraction lengthening and
over the past 2-3 months, has been lengthened approximately
122 mm. She is brought to the operating room today for
removal of the distraction apparatus and insertion of a
vascularized fibular graft into the intercalated gap.

DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE:  With the patient on the operating
table in the supine position, with the head of the bed
elevated 10 degrees, general endotracheal anesthetic was
induced without difficulty. Due to the large unusual size of
her body and large size of her breasts, she was positioned
almost in the right lateral decubitus position with the right
leg pronated as much as possible for the fibular dissection.
Tourniquet was wrapped at the left upper humeral level for
dissection in the forearm and hand. Left arm was on an arm
board. After all of the appropriate monitoring lines, IV
lines, etc. Were placed, dissection started on the leg.

The leg was elevated, exsanguinated and the tourniquet at the
mid thigh level was inflated to 350 mmHg. The usual incision
was made along the line between the lateral malleolus and the
fibular head proximally. Only one large perforator was
identified by Doppler examination intraoperatively before the
incision was made. The dissection progressed through skin and
large layer of subcutaneous fat to the muscular fascia which
was then incised over the anterior compartment. This was then
peeled down to the inner muscular septum laterally.  At this
point, we confirmed the presence of one perforator and only
one other perforator was present and this was proximal just
distal to the fibular head. The interseptum was then detached
from the fibula laterally. The muscle cuff was then gently
removed from the periosteum.  Osteotomies were made
proximally and distally and then a distal to proximal
elevation of the fibula with incision of the interosseous
membrane both posteriorly and anteriorly was done. The
peroneal vessels were clipped distally and a much larger
segment of bone was harvested so that we could get as long a
vascular pedicle as possible. We anticipated some potential
problems with isolation of vessels in hand and in the forearm
and this was indeed what we found. The peroneal pedicles were
followed up to the common branch with the posterior tibia
and, at this point, it was ready for transfer.  The
tourniquet was released after approximately 90 minutes.

Simultaneously on the left hand, first the distraction
apparatus was removed.  All 6 pins were removed.  The
extremity was elevated, prepped with Betadine scrub and
Betadine paint and draped in the usual fashion. First the pin
tracks over the fifth metacarpal were curetted. They were
then completely excised. Skin flaps were then elevated in the
anterior and posterior aspects and closed primarily as a
plastic closure. The incision on the forearm coursed the
entire length of the forearm which had been distracted of a
substantial amount. Again, the sites of the pin tracts were
completely excised. The skin in this patient was much more
indurated and soft tissues were not as supple and pliable as
most and certainly not as supple and pliable as they were on
her leg. There was no gross edema but the tissue was just
somewhat indurated and it was much harder mobilizing the skin
flaps on the left hand and the leg area. Old scar, of course,
was excised.  Dissection progressed between the superficial
and deeper layer of abundant subcutaneous fat to mobilize the
skin. The intercalated gap of the fibula was very well
isolated and very well exposed. The bone regenerate had
developed approximately 1 inch on either side of the
osteotomy toward the central portion of the intercalated gap.
The profundus muscle bellies to the ulnar 3 fingers were
palmar. These were isolated from what was present in the
fibula and they certainly had been stretched considerably
during this long distraction. Subperiosteal elevation was
then done.  We then picked a long straight DCP reconstruction
plate from the Synthes set and, with the tourniquet released,
this was fixed with three 4.0 mm cortical screws both
proximal and distal.  Care was taken to off set the plate so
that it was not lying directly on the incision and was
slightly more posterior to it.. With the plate intact, we
then elevated the arm,  re-exsanguinated the arm and turned
up the tourniquet. The ulnar artery had been isolated with
the ulnar nerve in the forearm and this was judged to be
satisfactory. We ideally wanted to convert a micro surgical
problem into a macro surgical one by getting much larger
vessels in the antecubital fossa.  The fossa was exposed with
a transverse incision in the elbow flexion crease. Very
meticulous dissection was done here. Several veins in the
antecubital region were prepared and interestingly, there was
no brachial artery in the normal position. We did not go deep
into the muscle layers and decided to use the arteries. The
artery on the forearm was an end-to-side anastomosis.  We
then had a vein pedicle extending up into the antecubital
region.  Enough of the veins in the antecubital region were
followed into the forearm through this incision as far as
possible so that we would have enough length on both sides,
which we did. However, there was no extra and I'm glad we did
this. With the tourniquet released, the peroneal artery was
anastomosed end-to-side into the ulnar artery at the mid
forearm level. During th dissection, the muscle was in slight
spasm with application of papaverine.  It dilated remarkedly
well and was a good medium sized vessel. End-to-side
anastomosis with simple everting interrupted 9-0 nylon
sutures was uncomplicated and with clamp release, there was
immediate excellent flow into the fibular graft. At this
point,  the forearm posterior incision was closed in layers
using two 3-0 and 4-0 buried Vicryl sutures. Because of the
tightness of the soft tissue, it was not possible to close
the middle third of this wound,  which later in the procedure
was covered with a VAC dressing. The venous pedicle was then
passed over the ulnar nerve which was well mobilized.  Under
the profundus muscles to the ulnar 3 fingers and then through
a subcutaneous tunnel to the antecubital fossa. They were
secured here. The venous leash was then brought up to the
recipient veins. The 2 venous anastomoses were done. One was
large-caliber in the  3-4 mm range with asymmetry which was
gradually dealt with by very careful placement of sutures.
The second vein was 3 mm and was directed end-to-end
anastomosis with 9-0 nylon sutures. No couplers were used.
With the clamp released, there was excellent capillary refill
to all portions of the flap itself. Of the vascularized bone,
no skin portions were included. The sponge count was correct.
Needle count was correct.  The lap count was correct.  The
background count was correct. At this point, we just checked
the antecubital region to make sure that the large clamp had
been removed. The antecubital wound was then closed in layers
using 3-0 and 4-0 buried Vicryl sutures. Penrose drain exited
the medial aspect of the wound. Light compression dressing
was applied. The PIP joints of the ulnar 3 fingers was then
pinned in more extension than normal as they had flexed
during the distraction process. These were held with oblique
.035 C wires in each digit. They were not completely extended
but they are at -35 degrees. When all of the wounds had been
closed, she was then immobilized with a posterior plaster
splint.  A VAC dressing was placed on the forearm.  A
decision has been made to leave the middle third of the wound
open and perform either a delayed primary closure or a
secondary skin graft. She tolerated all of these procedures
quite well.

be given IV antibiotics and pain medication.
